title: How a Card Payment Works: Issuer, Acquirer, Network, Processor

questions.question: A terminal displays "Approved" 1.2 seconds after a card tap. Which statement about the money is true at that moment?
options: The merchant's bank account has been credited with the purchase amount
The network has moved the funds from the issuer to the acquirer
The issuer has placed a hold on the cardholder's funds; nothing has moved
The cardholder's account has been debited and the merchant is paid at midnight
questions.explanation: Authorization is a real-time promise backed by a hold on the cardholder's open-to-buy or available balance. Money moves only at settlement, after the merchant clears the transaction, typically a day or more later. The last option describes a single-message PIN debit posting, which is not what a credit tap does, and even there the merchant is funded by the acquirer later, not at midnight.

questions.question: Which party pays interchange, and to whom?
options: The acquirer pays it to the issuer, out of the merchant discount it collects
The merchant pays it directly to the network as a scheme assessment
The issuer pays it to the acquirer as a reward for bringing volume
The cardholder pays it to the issuer as part of the annual card fee
questions.explanation: Interchange flows from acquirer to issuer on every cleared transaction and is netted at settlement; the acquirer recovers it from the merchant through the merchant discount rate. The network's own fee is the assessment, a separate and much smaller line, so the second option confuses two different fees.

questions.question: An acquirer sends a 0100 authorization request and receives no response before its timeout. What must it do?
options: Resend the identical 0100 until a 0110 arrives, since duplicates are harmless
Treat the transaction as approved under stand-in rules and clear it that night
Return response code 51 to the merchant so the customer tries another card
Send a 0400 reversal with the same STAN so any hold the issuer placed is released
questions.explanation: After a timeout the acquirer cannot know whether the issuer approved and placed a hold, so it sends a reversal, retrying from a store-and-forward queue until acknowledged. Resending the 0100 could create a second hold; only the network, not the acquirer, may approve under stand-in; and 51 is an issuer decision about funds, not a connectivity signal.

questions.question: In a dual-message system, why can the cleared amount legitimately differ from the authorized amount?
options: Because the network recalculates every amount in the issuer's billing currency during the clearing cycle
Because clearing is a separate later message carrying the final amount, and scheme rules allow tips, estimates, and partial captures
Because the issuer rounds authorization amounts to whole dollars and the clearing record restores the exact cents
Because the 0110 response only confirms that the card is valid and never carries any amount field at all
questions.explanation: Authorization and clearing are separate flows at separate times; the clearing record carries the final amount, and scheme rules permit differences such as a 20% tip tolerance, hotel estimates, and partial or multiple captures. FX conversion does happen at clearing, but it produces a billing-currency amount, not a different transaction amount, and single-message systems have no such gap at all.

questions.question: A 100.00 USD purchase has interchange of 1.80% + 0.10 USD, a network assessment of 0.13%, and a merchant discount rate of 2.50%. In cents, what do the issuer, network, and acquirer keep, and what does the merchant receive?
options: Issuer 190, network 13, acquirer 47, merchant 9750
Issuer 250, network 13, acquirer 0, merchant 9737
Issuer 180, network 10, acquirer 60, merchant 9750
Issuer 190, network 13, acquirer 250, merchant 9547
questions.explanation: Interchange is 180 + 10 = 190 cents to the issuer, the assessment is 13 cents to the network, the merchant pays 250 cents of discount and receives 9750, and the acquirer keeps the spread 250 - 190 - 13 = 47. The parties sum to 10000. The last option double-counts the discount as acquirer income on top of interchange and assessment.

questions.question: A PIN debit transaction on a single-message network is approved with a 0210. Which capability from the dual-message world does NOT exist here?
options: Sending a 0400 reversal if the terminal never printed a receipt
Routing the request to the issuer by the card's BIN range
Capturing a smaller amount than was approved when an item is out of stock
Receiving a response code that distinguishes insufficient funds from an invalid card
questions.explanation: In a single-message system the 0200/0210 both authorizes and clears, so the amount is final on approval; there is no later capture, partial or otherwise, and a change requires a reversal and a new transaction. Reversals, BIN routing, and detailed response codes exist on both kinds of rail.
